note:
v1, THE SKELETON of the third song, "PLAIN HUNT" (Harry: "answered clips. unlock a third track slot!"). The whole shape is standing, bare; no voice yet.
THE IDEA: a third kind of long cycle. English church bells cannot play tunes; ringers ring CHANGES: the bells strike once each, in a row, and from one row to the next a bell may only swap places with its neighbour, by a rule that visits every possible order exactly once and comes back to where it began. Here the riff is that row: six sixteenths, five notes that change places (Eb C B Ab Gb, the album's hook notes running down) and a low F that always comes last. It is rung through two whole cycles, 240 rows, no two alike within either, and each ends on the scale it began on. The highest note walks later and later through the riff and back, all piece long; the kick goes with it and a church bell doubles it.
THE SHAPE (5:05): 0:00 church bells alone ring the scale down, slowly. 0:10 the band takes it up at twice the speed. 0:25 the order starts to change: the first cycle, on F, then up to A flat (1:02), then B (1:40), the drums harder each time. 2:17 it has come round: one chord, and the bells alone again. 2:37 the second cycle, by a different rule, on F, A flat (3:15) and C (3:52). 4:30 the landing: the scale again on F, with the bells ringing it over the band at half speed. 4:52 one chord, and the lowest bell tolls three times.

note:
v5, THE ROW BECOMES A RIFF (whole song). Through v4 the riff was six even sixteenths: a run of notes. A riff has weight. Now two of its notes do, wherever they stand:
- the HIGHEST note is LONG: open and ringing (two sixteenths in the first cycle, three in the second);
- the LOW F that always comes last is REPEATED: two muted chugs in the first cycle, three in the second, a gallop;
- the four notes between are single muted sixteenths, as before.
So in the first cycle the riff is half a bar long: every one starts on a beat, the two low chugs close each half bar, and the long note slides later and later through it, then earlier and earlier, against a beat that does not move. In the second cycle the riff is ten sixteenths: heavier, and it turns against the bar (they meet every fifth bar). The order of the notes still follows the bell-ringers' rule, the same 240 rows. The song is faster (120 for 96) so a riff takes about the time it took, and the landing is played as the band first played it.
THE SHAPE NOW (5:24): 0:00 bells; 0:08 the band; 0:16 the first cycle (up to A flat at 0:56, B at 1:36); 2:16 it comes round: gong, bells over the chant; 2:32 the second cycle on the bass alone, guitars at 2:42 (A flat 3:22, C 4:12, the lead climbs from 4:18); 5:02 the landing; 5:18 the last chord.

note:
v6, THE METHOD IS HEARD (whole song). Through v5 the two long stretches were a riff that kept changing over a kit that did not: nothing told you where you were. The bell-ringers' method has a shape, and now the band plays it:
- HOME: every ten riffs the long note comes back to the front of the riff, twice running. A crash now goes on each of those two long notes, and the kit no longer crashes by counting bars. In the first cycle that is every five bars (0:24, 0:34, 0:44 ...); in the second every six and a quarter, so each one falls a beat later in the bar (2:42, 3:07, 3:32 ...).
- THE CALL: where a ringer would shout a change of course (three times in the first cycle, six in the second) the whole band plays those two riffs as a break in unison: every note open and loud, and the drummer stops the beat and plays the riff on the kit (a crash for the long note, four toms high to low for the four notes between, the snare for the low chugs). First cycle: 0:54, 1:34, 2:14, each the bar before the key moves. Second cycle: 2:54, 3:19, 3:44, 4:09, 4:34 and 4:59, the last straight into the landing.
- THE RIFF LAID BARE: once in each cycle, as the key moves up to A flat (0:56-1:06 and 3:22-3:34), the guitars play only the long note and the low chugs, and the bass alone keeps the notes between. You hear the long note slide against the chugs with nothing in the way; then the whole riff comes back.

v13, THE BELL IN THE HUNT (section round, 2:40-3:12, as drawn: the second cycle's first stretch, which the map called static: twenty-five bars of the riff on F under one beat).
The second cycle of this song rings Grandsire, and what makes Grandsire itself is that TWO bells hunt: the treble (the riff's long note, which you already hear walking through the row) and one more, "the bell in the hunt", which walks through the row with it. And what a call does in Grandsire is put a different bell into the hunt. Through twelve versions only the treble's walk could be heard.
Now, from 2:44, the bell in the hunt is heard too: its note is left open on the guitars, and the drummer strikes it on that bell's own tom (the toms the kit already rings the calls on). So each row has two accents, and they walk through the row against each other, cross, and part. After the call at 2:55 the second accent is on another note and another tom: the third bell has gone into the hunt in place of the second. It runs to the next call at 3:19.
